extracted.intended_audience: news editors, journalists, publishers, and media regulators
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and guidance for homepage headlines and linked articles to ensure fairness, balance and to avoid causing substantial offence or prejudice—especially when referencing religion or ethnicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure factual material is presented with reasonable fairness and balance (General Principle 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications must take reasonable steps to ensure that factual material in news material is presented with reasonable fairness and balance, and that writers’ expressions of opinion are not based on significantly inaccurate factual material or omission of key facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable steps include making clear context and source of allegations or threats (e.g., whether a threat is an individual's social-media comment). Failure to make such distinctions can constitute a breach (example: homepage headline implying a religion was responsible when the material referred to an individual comment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid causing or contributing materially to substantial offence, distress or prejudice (General Principle 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications must take reasonable steps to avoid causing or contributing materially to substantial offence, distress or prejudice, or a substantial risk to health or safety, unless doing so is sufficiently in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting on sensitive topics (religion, ethnicity, etc.), weigh public interest justifications carefully. Prominent wording that suggests collective responsibility for violence where none is established can cause substantial prejudice and is not justified absent strong public interest. The Council found a breach where the homepage item did not make clear the limitation of responsibility and so contributed to prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prominent references to religious or ethnic groups in headlines that imply collective responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Prominent references to religious or ethnic groups in headlines can imply that a group, as a whole, is responsible for the actions of a minority among that group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take reasonable steps to identify the particular sources of violence or threats as clearly as possible (for example, specifying an individual actor, a social-media post, or an identified group). Avoid wording in headlines (especially emphatic words like 'DARK' or 'THREAT' next to a religion/ethnicity) that unfairly suggests collective culpability. Training and editorial checks on headline wording are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make clear the provenance and scope of alleged threats or violent acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting must make it sufficiently clear when purported threats or violent acts are limited to an individual's comment (e.g., on social media) rather than the belief or actions of a religion or community as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to state that a purported 'Islamic threat' was a comment on social media (rather than an organised movement or the religion itself) led the Council to find a breach of fairness and balance. Explicitly indicate source (social-media comment, individual, organisation) in headline or immediate subhead/lede where prominence could otherwise mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homepage/headline responsibility — prominence matters regardless of linked article wording
rubrics_metrics.description: A homepage headline that links to an article with a different, more accurate headline does not absolve the publication of responsibility for the homepage wording while it is prominent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must ensure homepage headlines themselves meet standards of fairness and balance, because prominent homepage text may be seen by readers independently of the linked article. Relying on the article headline (which may differ) is not an adequate defence if the homepage wording is misleading or prejudicial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial processes and training on use of religious terms in headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications should educate and train homepage editors on appropriate use of religious terms in headlines to prevent misleading or prejudicial wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The publication in this case acknowledged that wording was 'clumsy' and said it had shared the Council’s guidelines on the use of ‘Religious terms in headlines’ with homepage editors. The Council welcomed steps to educate editors — implying that proactive training and editorial guidelines are a recommended mitigation and best practice.
